nameStory: The name 'perfoliate' comes from Latin meaning 'through the leaf' - if you look closely, the stem appears to pierce right through the middle of the upper leaves! 'Penny-cress' refers to the small, round, coin-like seed pods that develop after flowering. It's like nature created its own tiny currency scattered along the stem.
description: Perfoliate penny-cress is a small annual herb in the mustard family that grows 6-18 inches tall. It has distinctive heart-shaped upper leaves that wrap around the stem so completely that the stem appears to pass right through them. The plant produces clusters of tiny white flowers followed by small, round, flattened seed pods. As a non-native species from Europe and Asia, it's quite rare in New England with only a couple of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Upper leaves are heart-shaped and clasp the stem so completely that the stem appears to pierce through the leaf blade - this perfoliate feature is unmistakable when present

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in loose clusters at the stem tips, each flower only about 1/8 inch across with a faint sweet scent

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive round, flattened seed pods about the size of a small coin, with a notched tip and papery texture when ripe

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Smooth, hairless annual plant growing 6-18 inches tall with an upright, branching stem that feels firm and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are oval and stalked while upper leaves become increasingly heart-shaped and stem-clasping, all with smooth edges and a slightly waxy feel

habitat: This rare plant is typically found in disturbed soils, waste places, and along roadsides where the ground has been recently turned. It prefers well-drained, often rocky or gravelly soils in sunny locations. In its native range it grows in agricultural areas and disturbed ground, so in New England look for it in similar human-modified habitats.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants develop their characteristic lower leaves, beginning to show the stem-clasping feature on emerging upper leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs with tiny white blooms appearing in clusters, followed by the development of the distinctive round, coin-like seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open to release seeds, while the annual plant begins to die back and turn brown.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain as this is an annual plant, but seeds may persist in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: The perfoliate leaves create such a perfect seal around the stem that rainwater can collect in the leaf cups, essentially turning each leaf into a tiny reservoir that helps the plant survive dry spells!
confusionNotes: The perfoliate leaf arrangement is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other plants when this feature is present. However, young plants before the upper leaves develop might be mistaken for other mustard family members - look for the smooth, waxy leaves and remember that the diagnostic stem-piercing leaves will appear as the plant matures.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'penny-cress,' this plant was recently moved from the genus Thlaspi to Noccaea based on genetic studies, so you may still see it listed as Thlaspi perfoliatum in older field guides. The 'cress' in the name refers to its membership in the mustard family, though it's not closely related to watercress or garden cress.
compareHints: As the only Noccaea species in New England, compare it to other mustard family members like field pennycress (Thlaspi arvense), which has similar round seed pods but lacks the distinctive perfoliate leaves. The stem-clasping, heart-shaped upper leaves of perfoliate penny-cress are unique among our regional mustards and make identification straightforward when present.
